The affair comes as Nvidia, valued at about $5 trillion, faces doubts over the sustainability of a massive spending boom and a sell-off in related stocks. Huang has lobbied Trump to ease chip export restrictions on China, and the sales deal has been slowed by strict licence reviews. Analysts said Huang’s influence could be weakened, and that the company depends heavily on him, with no obvious successor.
items.cav: The espionage claims come from press reports citing US officials, and the officials have not commented publicly. Nvidia’s conclusion that secrets were not compromised is its own view and has not been tested by the investigation. Some details, including the memo and Trump’s briefing, rest on second-hand reporting.
items.op: A chipmaker’s chief executive is not above scrutiny when national security may be at stake. Nvidia’s investigation is a start, but its findings should be made public as far as possible. Shareholders and the public deserve to know whether a foreign power gained access to sensitive technology, not only whether the company is comfortable with its own answer.

items.t: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang faces questions over alleged Chinese espionage link
items.s: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether chief executive Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The allegations centre on a Chinese businesswoman, and the company’s shares fell more than 4 percent in overnight trading.
p: Scrutiny has landed on Nvidia’s chief executive after reports that a Chinese woman he had a romantic involvement with may have been collecting information for Beijing. Huang, who helped found the chipmaker more than thirty years ago, has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. The firm, however, says it sees no grounds to think sensitive US material or proprietary data has been exposed.

The board has commissioned a review, led by a committee of directors with outside lawyers, to establish whether Huang was the subject of a foreign spying effort. The inquiry followed media coverage tying him to Alice Huang, who previously worked as an executive at a data centre firm based in Singapore. Reports indicate the two are not related, despite sharing a surname. Huang has pledged to cooperate and to keep leading the company.

The claims originated with a New York Times investigation published last month. That outlet cited American intelligence officials who believed Beijing had enlisted Alice Huang to learn about the chief executive and perhaps sway Nvidia’s chip sales into China. Exactly what she obtained, whether anything sensitive reached Chinese hands, and how much Huang understood about any scheme are still unknown.

Huang told Bloomberg News in late October that his dealings with her were tied to Megaspeed, her company, and were ordinary. According to the Times, Megaspeed became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying roughly $4.8bn of equipment. American authorities have reportedly examined Megaspeed since 2024, suspecting it helped China acquire top Nvidia processors despite export controls. No criminal charges against either Huang have been reported.

Alice Huang, also called Huang Le, has not commented on the espionage allegations, and her whereabouts are unknown. An entry in a Chinese investment database lists earlier roles at HSBC and Chinese broadcasters, though AFP said it could not verify those details independently.

Politicians from both major parties are weighing in. Republican members of Congress have asked Huang to appear before lawmakers on 18 November, arguing that China’s possible access to sensitive American technology is at stake. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers from the company and urged passage of tougher rules to keep advanced US technology away from China.

Investors reacted quickly, with Nvidia’s market value of $4.5 trillion sliding more than 4 percent in overnight trading into Monday. Chris Beauchamp of IG Group said it was too early to tell whether the episode would prove a “major turning point” for the company.
items.cav: The sources do not establish what information, if any, was passed to Beijing, nor what Huang knew. Much of the espionage account rests on anonymous US intelligence officials as reported by the New York Times, and details of Alice Huang’s background are unverified. Her side of the story has not been heard.
items.op: Allegations of foreign espionage touching a company central to US chip policy are a matter of public interest, not private scandal. The independent review and congressional testimony should be conducted in the open, with findings published. Investors, lawmakers and the public deserve clear answers rather than assurances from the company.

items.t: Four killed in Gaza as sand embankment collapses onto displaced families’ tents after heavy rain
items.s: Four people, including three children, died when a sand embankment fell onto tents at a displaced families’ camp in central Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. The collapse came after heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across the territory.
p: The health ministry says a woman and three children were killed on Sunday night when earth piled up in a sand embankment gave way onto tents at a camp south of Deir al-Balah. Five people were reportedly pulled out alive after the collapse.

The disaster followed torrential rain the previous day, which reportedly swamped tens of thousands of tents throughout Gaza and left many displaced Palestinians with nowhere dry to sleep. According to the Civil Defence service, water reached depths of up to 1.5 metres in places, and its responders could attend to just 10% of the 2,100 emergency calls they received.

Footage circulated online showed people searching for survivors by the light of mobile phones, picking through boulders, sand and crushed tents. Mustafa al-Masri, a rescuer, told the BBC that the rescue crews and young men from the camp had to reach the trapped people by hand, because the mound was so large and spread so wide that nobody knew how to start.

The official count has changed. The Civil Defence first said that two women and three children had died, but on Monday morning the health ministry said only one woman was among the dead. The names it has given are Tahrir Nabhan, Mariam Nabhan, her brother Salah and Habiba al-Zein.

The Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, urged international bodies to supply secure shelters and relocate tents away from sandy ground, slopes and any spot prone to collapse. Karl Baker of the International Organization for Migration described the aid now entering Gaza as far too limited, comparing it to the most minimal of plasters and calling for more donations in kind and funding.

Cogat, the Israeli military unit that coordinates aid deliveries, said more than 91,000 tents and other supplies had reached Gaza under its winter preparation scheme. It also said Israel would bar any equipment that Hamas or other armed factions could use for military ends. The UN estimates that roughly 80% of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed or damaged, and that 1.2 million of the more than 1.9 million displaced people live in tents or improvised shelters.

Masri said he had been forced out of Beit Hanoun in the north but remained in central Gaza, having found no other place he considered suitable. The UN warns that conditions stay grave despite the October 2025 ceasefire, as Israeli strikes keep hitting populated areas.
items.cav: The casualty figures differ between sources: the Civil Defence first reported five deaths, while the health ministry later reported four, and the sources do not explain the revision in detail. Both the health ministry and the Civil Defence operate under Hamas-run authorities, and the Cogat figures on deliveries are the Israeli military’s own claims that the sources do not independently verify.
items.op: Shelter for displaced families should not depend on whether a camp happens to sit below an unstable mound. The shift from five reported deaths to four shows why early figures from every side need checking against clear records. Disputes over what aid may enter should be settled openly, with published rules, not left to be argued through statements after each tragedy.

items.t: Krakow shooting: surgeons who were lunching nearby describe treating gunman and officers
items.s: Two surgeons who were eating near Krakow’s Main Market Square when a gunman opened fire say they treated the attacker and two police officers at the scene. One colleague says his actions undoubtedly saved an officer’s life.
p: Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families on Saturday when they heard gunshots, according to local media reports cited by the BBC. The shooting killed six people and injured 15, the BBC reported.

Pędziwiatr told the Polish outlet Fakt that his son ran up to him and said people were being shot and falling to the ground. When the two doctors reached the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers who had been shot while subduing him.

Wierdak worked on an officer who had been shot in the chest. Describing the emergency treatment, he told Fakt that he “stuffed all the bandages” into the wound. He said that without this, “I don’t know how things would have turned out”, because an ambulance had a long wait to arrive.

Pędziwiatr said he telephoned John Paul II Hospital, where the thoracic and cardiac surgery department is based, and insisted the officer be taken there. In his view, it offered the best chance of survival because specialists there treated that type of injury.

The two officers have been named as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański. On Sunday they came out of comas. Prime Minister Donald Tusk had earlier hailed both as heroes for preventing further deaths. (The BBC report describes the prime minister’s praise as “true heroes”; the officers’ recovery is reported by the BBC but details of their condition beyond this are not given in the evidence.)

Prosecutors said the 25-year-old Polish attacker remains in critical condition. They had earlier said he was inspired by “far-right ideologies” and have opened a terror investigation. The National Public Prosecutor’s Office is leading the inquiry through a unit that handles terrorist offences. The attacker is a suspect and has not been tried.

Among the dead were a British national and an Austrian woman, along with four Poles. Six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers, who were on a city break nearby, also gave medical help after the shooting, RTÉ News reported, quoting officer James McConnell. They provided CPR and haemorrhage control.

Witnesses described panic in the square. London resident Ruby Catherine Warren said she heard gunfire and ran with her friends until they reached a hotel to hide. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, said he was inside a nearby McDonald’s when he heard multiple gunshots, and later saw a body covered in foil blankets about 20 metres away.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the attacker acted alone, and the “far-right” motive is a prosecutors’ statement made before any trial. Several details, including the surgeons’ accounts, come through local media reports and may not be fully verified.
items.op: Heroism at the scene deserves praise, but it should not end the story. Prosecutors must explain the motive and the attacker’s path clearly, and the public deserves a transparent account of how the response unfolded.

items.t: Eisenkot Begins Bid to Form Israeli Government Without a Clear Majority
items.s: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has been given the mandate to form Israel’s next government, despite his bloc lacking a clear majority in parliament. He says Benjamin Netanyahu has brought the country to a historic crisis.
p: Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to allies of Benjamin Netanyahu. He said the veteran prime minister had led the country into a historic crisis.

Eisenkot, 66, leads the Yashar party and has promised to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation. President Isaac Herzog formally gave him a mandate and 28 days to build a government, even though his bloc does not have a clear majority. Herzog can grant a 14-day extension before the mandate must pass to someone else.

Speaking at a ceremony at the presidential office, Eisenkot said the country was “approaching a point of no return.” He called for a “national emergency government” and said it would require “creative and unconventional political steps.”

According to the Guardian, Eisenkot has three possible routes. He could agree a power-sharing deal with Netanyahu, win support from Arab-led parties, which several members of his own bloc oppose, or reach an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, who want military exemptions for their community.

The October election left neither side with a majority. Eisenkot’s opposition bloc won 48 of the 120 seats, while Netanyahu’s camp took 53. Both Arab-majority lists endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog, and they could now act as kingmakers. Eisenkot has set conditions for any Arab party joining his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and labelling Hamas a terrorist organisation. The more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party has already said it will not sit with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot has also appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud and to the far-right party of finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, but only on the condition that he serve as prime minister. Netanyahu called for a national unity government with Eisenkot on Saturday, though it is unclear whether the two can agree on power sharing. Netanyahu is expected to keep up pressure, warning that any alliance with Arab parties would be a betrayal.

Netanyahu has repeatedly said the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, but the Guardian reports he has offered little to no evidence. Israel’s Shin Bet security agency is investigating possible foreign interference. The Central Elections Committee and Herzog say the vote was valid, and that any wrongdoing found would not have changed the result significantly.

Eisenkot, who was military chief from 2015 to 2019, has vowed to crack down on extremist settlers in the West Bank and has described recent attacks as Jewish terror. He opposes a Palestinian state and wants to end Hamas rule in Gaza. If he cannot assemble a coalition, Israel faces fresh elections, having already held five between 2019 and 2022.
items.cav: The Guardian is the detailed source here; the second outlet’s brief summary adds only that Eisenkot has up to six weeks, which matches the 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu’s claim of a stolen election is his own and is not supported by the evidence; the outcome of the Shin Bet investigation is not reported.
items.op: Israel’s coalition arithmetic should not override the basic question of how the vote was run and who is accountable for it. Netanyahu’s unsupported fraud claims make transparent answers from the Shin Bet and the elections committee more urgent. Any coalition, whoever leads it, must be judged by whether it restores public trust.

items.t: Collision of two trains south of Cairo kills at least seven, officials say
items.s: Officials say at least seven people died and over a hundred were hurt when two trains struck each other on Sunday south of Cairo. Egypt’s president has called for a swift inquiry.
p: The collision took place in al-Ayyat, a district of Giza province roughly 30 miles south of Cairo. Citing the transport ministry, reports say a service bound for Fayoum, in the south-west, slammed into the back of a train that was headed for Aswan, in the south.

Officials said an inspection showed the Cairo-Aswan train was standing still on that same line when the impact occurred. The reporting does not explain why it was stopped there, or how the other train ended up on that track.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat, told the Guardian that bystanders hurried over, dragged survivors out and summoned ambulances. He claimed to have watched around 80 casualties being driven to hospital, and said some travellers were caught in a carriage of the motionless train and did not survive.

In a post on social media, President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi said he had instructed investigators to act quickly. The Egyptian railway authority said rescue crews and cranes were deployed to remove the debris and bring services back to timetable as soon as possible.

Rail accidents are a recurring problem in Egypt, where the network has been criticised for poor management and inadequate equipment upkeep. Authorities have launched modernisation programmes in recent years. In September, two freight trains crashed in the same district, leaving the driver and his assistant injured.
The country’s worst rail tragedy remains the 2002 blaze on an overnight train from Cairo to southern Egypt, which claimed more than 300 lives.
items.cav: The death toll of at least seven and the figure of more than 100 injured come from officials; the claim of 80 hospital transfers comes from one resident’s account. The cause of the collision has not been established, and the reporting does not say whether the findings will be made public.
items.op: Seven deaths and more than 100 injuries require more than a routine promise of inquiry. The investigation the president ordered should publish its findings, explain why a stationary train was struck on the same track, and name any maintenance failures. Repeated crashes make openness the only credible answer.

items.t: More than 200 tarantula sightings reported in Austria since September
items.s: Austrian citizens have reported more than 200 tarantula sightings since early September, and experts have verified 175 of them. Most reports come from Styria, Lower Austria and Burgenland.
p: Austria has logged more than 200 tarantula sightings over roughly two months, according to reports gathered through naturbeobachtung.at, a citizen science platform. Experts have verified 175 of them.
By region, Styria in the southeast leads with 66 reports. Lower Austria counted 49 and Burgenland 43, while Carinthia also registered sightings.

Autumn is the busiest season for the spiders, which look for protected spots to pass the winter. Occasionally they end up inside homes, apartments and garages. In nature they normally retreat to burrows dug underground and to cracks in rocks.

Among the standout finds was a South Russian tarantula in Tulln, Lower Austria, well to the northwest of its usual range. Carolina Trcka-Rojas of the Austrian Nature Conservation Association said no sightings had previously been recorded in that surrounding area. In late August, a black-bellied tarantula turned up in Stossau, in the lower Gail valley, the species' westernmost known Austrian record.

Two tarantula species are generally found in Austria. Both belong to the wolf spider group and may bite when provoked, an event described as uncommon. A bite can hurt and leave redness and swelling, but it is generally not dangerous for healthy adults.

Historical records place the first documented South Russian tarantula in Austria in the early 1920s, near Lake Neusiedl and Vienna. The black-bellied species was first recorded in Styria during the 1970s.
Austria is not alone in this trend. A 2025 study reported that tarantulas in Czechia are spreading again after decades of decline, and researchers point to warmer, drier summers as a major factor.
items.cav: The figures come from a citizen science platform, so they reflect reported sightings rather than measured population changes, and the sources do not say whether the tarantula population is actually growing. The Austrian counts are not broken down by species.
items.op: Open citizen data helps scientists track wildlife, but it should be read with care. Authorities and researchers should publish clear methods and verified counts, so that public alarm does not outrun the evidence.

items.t: Diwali lights up India as air pollution clouds the festival in Delhi and Mumbai
items.s: Millions across India are marking Diwali with lamps, fireworks and sweets, but the celebrations are taking place amid rising concern about air quality, especially in the north. The Supreme Court has allowed certified “green” firecrackers in Delhi for a limited period.
p: Across India, millions of people are taking part in Diwali, a Hindu festival held on a moonless night in the month of Kartik. Homes, shrines, workplaces and public streets glow with lamps and bright lights, a display meant to represent the defeat of darkness by illumination.

Customs vary from region to region and from community to community, yet most celebrations include prayer, get-togethers at home, sweets shared among relatives and friends, and firecrackers. In the days beforehand, people tidy and adorn their houses with flowers and clay lamps called diyas, colourful floor designs appear at doorways, and shops fill with buyers.

According to the BBC, the festivities are overshadowed by worsening air quality, particularly in northern India. Weather patterns and the burning of crop stubble are cited as contributing factors, and fireworks set off during the holiday can add to the problem. Delhi's pollution has reached hazardous levels, which the broadcaster describes as the worst Diwali for air in a decade, and recent measures do not appear to have worked. Mumbai, the financial capital, has also recorded high readings in recent weeks.

India's Supreme Court, ruling on Monday, granted a temporary exemption allowing certified “green” firecrackers to be made, sold and set off in Delhi and nearby areas. These devices are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. Critics doubt how much they help, and they worry that ordinary firecrackers could still reach the capital from neighbouring states.

Beyond the fireworks, the festival commemorates Lord Ram's return to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the chief villain of the Ramayana epic. The celebrations unfold over several days. Dhanteras, which began on 6 November, is a day for buying gold, silver or new utensils, considered lucky. Chhoti Diwali brings lamps and, in some homes, firecrackers. The main day involves evening prayers to Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, followed by festive meals. The final day, Bhai Dooj, honours the bond between brothers and sisters.

Sikhs and Jains also mark the period. Sikhs commemorate the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th century. For Jains, the day is linked to Lord Mahavira's attainment of moksha, or liberation from rebirth. Indian communities abroad hold their own gatherings and exchange gifts.

The occasion is also seen as a favourable time for new purchases. India's stock exchanges will hold a one-hour special trading session, known as Muhurat trading, on 8 November this year. In Nepal, where the festival is called Tihar, pets and street animals are honoured.
items.cav: The source does not say how the “most polluted in a decade” judgement was measured or by whom, and it gives no current air quality readings. The 20-30% emissions figure for green firecrackers comes without independent testing details, and the critics' objections are reported without specifics.
items.op: Celebration should not come at the cost of breathable air for millions of residents. If pollution rules are to mean anything, the court's temporary permission must be paired with transparent monitoring and enforcement, so that citizens can see whether the measures are working.

items.t: Herzog taps Gadi Eisenkot to try forming Israel’s next government
items.s: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has asked Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to attempt to build a government after an October election left neither him nor Benjamin Netanyahu with a clear route to power. If Eisenkot succeeds, he would replace Netanyahu as prime minister.
p: Isaac Herzog has selected Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and the most prominent challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu, to attempt to assemble a cabinet. According to the president’s office, Herzog told Eisenkot of his decision late on Saturday. The formal handover was scheduled for a ceremony on Sunday at the presidential residence in Jerusalem.

The Knesset has been stalemated since the vote on 27 October, when Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist alliance lost its parliamentary majority. Even so, his camp won 53 of the 120 seats, the largest share in the chamber. Eisenkot’s opposition grouping took 48, so neither side reaches the 61 seats needed to govern.

Eisenkot, 66 and a former army chief, wrote on X that the moment called for a government of national urgency. He also received the backing of both Arab-majority lists, which posted record results and could now decide who governs. Analysts in the sources describe three possible paths: a power-sharing arrangement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties, or a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties that want military exemptions for their community.

The route ahead is difficult. Eisenkot has attached conditions to any Arab party joining his coalition, among them acknowledging Israel as a Jewish state and classifying Hamas as a terrorist group. Yisrael Beiteinu, one of his partners, has ruled out sitting in a government with Arab-led parties. Equal military service, including an end to the ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions, was a core theme of his campaign.

Netanyahu has repeatedly said Arab parties stole the election, yet the report says he has produced little to no proof. Israel’s Shin Bet security service has opened an inquiry into possible foreign meddling. The Central Elections Committee and Herzog maintain the vote was valid and that any irregularities would not have materially altered the outcome. Netanyahu has called for a unity government with Eisenkot, but it is unclear whether the two can agree terms on sharing power.

Eisenkot has promised to curb violent extremist settlers in the West Bank, whose attacks on Palestinians he has described as Jewish terror. He opposes a Palestinian state and has pledged to end Hamas’s control of Gaza. He has 28 days to gather a majority, and Herzog can extend that by 14 days. If no candidate succeeds, Israel faces another election.
items.cav: The sources do not establish whether Eisenkot can assemble a majority, and Netanyahu’s fraud claims remain unsupported by the evidence. The Shin Bet inquiry is ongoing, so its findings are unknown. The count of this as a sixth election since 2019 is an inference from the five elections the report mentions between 2019 and 2022.
items.op: Whoever governs Israel next will be judged on whether they respect the process that produced them. Unsubstantiated claims that an election was stolen erode public trust, and so do backroom deals dressed up as national unity. Israelis deserve a coalition built on open terms that can withstand scrutiny.
